title: Darts: overview
d: Darts is a target throwing sport played 1 per side.
definition: Darts is a target throwing sport played 1 per side.
description: Darts is a target throwing sport. be first to reach exactly zero from 501. The contest is played 1 per side, and the side that legs won by checkout; sets group legs; most sets wins wins. Modern game from English pubs; PDC/BDO split defined the pro era from 1993. The sport is governed by official laws that cover the field of play, equipment, players, officials, scoring, fouls, and conduct; this database walks through every one of those areas so a newcomer can follow a full match with understanding.

title: The objective
d: The objective of Darts is: be first to reach exactly zero from 501.
definition: The objective of Darts is: be first to reach exactly zero from 501.
description: Every rule in Darts exists to serve one objective: be first to reach exactly zero from 501. All tactics, positions, and scoring flow from that single aim. Beginners should fix the objective in mind first, because every foul, stoppage, and strategy in the sport is judged against whether it fairly advances or unfairly blocks that objective. Coaches return to it constantly: if a play does not serve the objective, it is the wrong play.

Scorekeepers record each score the moment it happens, and at most levels the scoreboard is the official record unless a protest is filed under the competition rules.

title: How games are won

definition: Darts: legs won by checkout; sets group legs; most sets wins.
description: Winning Darts comes down to the scoreboard: legs won by checkout; sets group legs; most sets wins. Because of that, late-game strategy everywhere in the sport is clock-and-score management — protecting a lead or chasing one changes every decision, from how much risk to take to when to slow play down or speed it up. Champions are often simply the teams that manage the winning condition best in the final minutes.

title: Ties and tiebreakers
d: Tied games in Darts are resolved under the competition rules for the level of play.
definition: Tied games in Darts are resolved under the competition rules for the level of play.
description: Not every contest in Darts can end tied: league games may allow draws while knockout games must produce a winner through extra time, tiebreak procedures, or shootouts defined by the competition. Tiebreak rules are announced before play and never invented mid-game; players and coaches must know them, because they reshape tactics — a team may play for penalties, or gamble everything to avoid them.

title: Match duration
d: Darts contests last: matches 30 minutes to 3 hours.
definition: Darts contests last: matches 30 minutes to 3 hours.
description: A Darts contest runs matches 30 minutes to 3 hours. Duration shapes fitness demands: athletes train to be sharp in the final stretch, not just the first. Timekeeping is an official duty — the clock, not the players, decides when it ends, and added or extra time exists to compensate for stoppages so the advertised duration is genuinely played.

title: Periods and breaks
d: Play in Darts is divided into periods with breaks as defined for the competition.
definition: Play in Darts is divided into periods with breaks as defined for the competition.
description: The matches 30 minutes to 3 hours in Darts give coaches their main lever: adjustments, substitutions, and rest happen in the breaks. Teams plan for three phases — start fast, manage the middle, finish strong — and the side that uses its breaks better often wins the second half. Break length and number are fixed by the rules; exceeding them can draw penalties.

title: Playing surface

definition: Darts surfaces must be safe, level, and marked to regulation.
description: The playing surface in Darts must be safe, level, and marked to regulation. Surface changes tactics: fast surfaces reward speed and quick passing, slow or soft ones reward power and patience. Footwear and equipment rules usually assume a specific surface, and playing on the wrong one risks both injury and disqualification of the contest.

description: No one plays Darts without: darts (max 50g), board. Equipment is inspected — illegal or unsafe gear is removed before play, and at higher levels every item must meet the governing body's specifications. Beginners should buy for safety and fit first, performance second; the right size matters more than the brand.

title: The ball

definition: The Darts ball is specified by the laws: size, weight, and pressure are regulated.

Ball specs change the whole game — a lighter, livelier ball rewards touch, a heavier one rewards power. Match balls are approved and often supplied by the competition; warming up with the wrong spec builds the wrong feel.

title: Protective gear
d: Protection in Darts: required and recommended gear keeps players safe within the laws.
definition: Protection in Darts: required and recommended gear keeps players safe within the laws.
description: Protection is part of the laws of Darts, not an afterthought. Required and recommended gear exists because the sport's known injury patterns are known: the rules mandate the gear that prevents the common ones. Gear must fit and be worn correctly — loose or missing protection can keep a player off the field, and no contest is worth a preventable injury.

title: Team size
d: Darts is played 1 per side.
definition: Darts is played 1 per side.
description: Darts is played 1 per side. Numbers decide the geometry of the game: more players means more structure and specialization, fewer means more space and versatility. Every player must know the legal team size, because playing short — or with too many — brings penalties, and planned rotations are built around the allowed numbers.

title: Positions and roles
d: Positions in Darts divide the work: each role has a zone, duties, and skills.
definition: Positions in Darts divide the work: each role has a zone, duties, and skills.
description: Positions in Darts exist to divide the 1 per side into manageable jobs. Each role has a home zone, primary duties, and a skill profile; great teams are built by fitting people to roles, not roles to people. Beginners should learn one position deeply before roaming — mastery of a role teaches the whole game faster than playing everywhere badly.

title: Substitutions
d: Substitution rules in Darts control how and when players may be replaced.
definition: Substitution rules in Darts control how and when players may be replaced.
description: Substitutions in Darts are a tactical weapon governed by strict procedure: only at stoppages, only through the official, only within the allowed number. Coaches plan substitution windows the way generals plan reserves — fresh legs at the right moment win tight games. Illegal substitution procedure can cost a team a player or a penalty.

title: Officials
d: Darts is officiated by: caller/scorer; referee in pro play.
definition: Darts is officiated by: caller/scorer; referee in pro play.
description: Darts is officiated by caller/scorer; referee in pro play. Officials are neutral arbiters of the laws: their decisions on matters of fact are final during play, and dissent is penalized. Knowing what each official watches helps players stay legal — most fouls are committed in full view of exactly the official assigned to that zone.

title: The referee's role
d: The referee in Darts enforces the laws, keeps time, and manages conduct.
definition: The referee in Darts enforces the laws, keeps time, and manages conduct.
description: The referee's job in Darts is bigger than blowing a whistle: enforcing the laws, keeping time, managing conduct, and protecting player safety — in that order. Players may ask for clarification respectfully; they may not dispute decisions. At every level, the referee's authority begins when they enter the venue and ends when they leave it.

title: Fouls
d: Illegal play in Darts draws fouls under the laws; persistent fouling draws cards or ejections.
definition: Illegal play in Darts draws fouls under the laws; persistent fouling draws cards or ejections.
description: A foul in Darts is illegal play as defined by the laws — not just rough play, but any act the rules forbid. Officials grade fouls by intent, danger, and advantage gained; persistent or cynical fouling draws escalating punishment. Smart players learn the exact line: physical right up to it, never across it.

title: Penalties
d: Fouls in Darts are punished by free plays, spot penalties, or loss of possession per the laws.
definition: Fouls in Darts are punished by free plays, spot penalties, or loss of possession per the laws.
description: Punishment in Darts fits the foul: minor infringements restart play for the other side, serious ones award direct scoring chances or remove the offender. Penalty rules are deliberately severe enough that fouling is never a good trade — the team that stays disciplined keeps eleven (or its equivalent) on the field and wins the close ones.

title: Discipline and conduct
d: Misconduct in Darts — dissent, dangerous play, unsporting behavior — is penalized, up to ejection.
definition: Misconduct in Darts — dissent, dangerous play, unsporting behavior — is penalized, up to ejection.
description: The laws of Darts punish misconduct on a ladder: warnings, cards, sin-bins, ejections, suspensions. Dissent, dangerous play, and unsporting behavior are treated as seriously as technical fouls, because the game depends on respect for officials and opponents. Captains are responsible for their team's conduct and speak to the referee for the side.

description: All Darts strategy serves the objective: be first to reach exactly zero from 501. The basic game plan is simple — win your individual battles, keep your shape, and take the chances the scoring system rewards most. Beginners win by doing simple things reliably; advanced players win by forcing opponents into mistakes while making none themselves.

title: Offense

definition: Attacking in Darts means creating the scoring chances the rules reward.
description: Attacking Darts is about manufacturing the highest-percentage chances the scoring system allows. Good offense is patient until the opening appears, then ruthless: create space, move the defense, and finish. The best attacks look simple because every player knows the plan two passes ahead.

The great defensive teams all share one trait: every player defends, all the time, without being asked.

title: Origins

Like most sports, it began as folk play and was formalized when clubs and schools wrote common rules so strangers could compete fairly. Those first written laws are the ancestor of every rule in this database — the game you watch today is their descendant.

title: Modern era

definition: Modern Darts: professional leagues, world championships, and Olympic or global stages.
description: Modern Darts grew through professional leagues, world championships, and global competition. Television and professionalism standardized the laws worldwide and turned the best players into full-time athletes. The modern game is faster, stronger, and more tactical than any earlier era — but it is played under the same essential objective the founders wrote down.

title: Variations
d: Darts has official and informal variations with adjusted rules for numbers, space, and level.
definition: Darts has official and informal variations with adjusted rules for numbers, space, and level.
description: Every major sport spawns variations: small-sided, beach, indoor, youth, and disability versions of Darts all adjust numbers, space, and rules while keeping the soul of the game. Variations are where most people actually play — the full eleven-a-side (or equivalent) version is the tip of a much bigger pyramid.

title: Safety
d: Play Darts safely: warm up, wear the required gear, follow the foul laws, and stop for injury.
definition: Play Darts safely: warm up, wear the required gear, follow the foul laws, and stop for injury.
description: Safety in Darts is part of the rules, not separate from them: warm up properly, wear every required piece of gear, respect the foul laws that exist to prevent injury, and stop play for any head injury or suspected serious harm. No game, drill, or tryout is worth playing hurt — the laws protect players who protect themselves.
